courses.name: Algorithms
courses.implementation: Prediction introduction, authored guidance, state walkthrough, existing topic lab and misconception notes

syllabus.title: Algorithmic thinking
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. An algorithm is a finite, precise procedure. State the input, required output and allowed operations before comparing solutions.

syllabus.title: Growth and bounds
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Count a basic operation as a function of input size. Constants affect actual speed, while eventual growth describes scalability.

syllabus.title: Counting work and input cases
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Count inner-body visits, including how the inner limit depends on the outer index. Two loops in sequence add work; fully nested independent loops multiply it.

syllabus.title: Recurrence trees
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. A recurrence separates recursive subproblem costs from local work. Specify a base case so repeated expansion terminates.

syllabus.title: Master theorem and its limits
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). The standard theorem requires fixed a>=1 and b>1 and applicable gap conditions.

syllabus.title: Transforming recurrences
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. For T(n)=T(sqrt(n))+1 on n>=2, let m=log2(n). Then S(m)=S(m/2)+1, so the original growth is Theta(log log n).

syllabus.title: Divide and combine
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Divide and conquer creates smaller instances, solves them, and combines their answers. A singleton base case prevents endless splitting.

syllabus.title: Stable merging
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Merge sort recursively sorts both halves, then merges the sorted results. Linear combine work across logarithmically many levels gives Theta(n log n).

syllabus.title: Bottom-up merging
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Bottom-up merge sort begins with sorted runs of length one and doubles the run width after each pass. No recursive call stack is needed.

syllabus.title: Many streams and storage
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. For k sorted streams containing N keys in total, keep one current head per nonempty stream in a min-heap. Each output updates one head, giving O(N log k) time.

syllabus.title: Extrema and comparison budgets
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. The second largest distinct item must be among those that lost directly to the maximum in a comparison tournament, assuming all keys are distinct.

syllabus.title: Inversions and ranking disagreement
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. An inversion is a pair of indices i<j with A[i]>A[j]. Equal values are not inversions. Reversing a sorted list of distinct keys maximizes the count.

syllabus.title: Geometry, powers and matrices
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. The closest pair may lie within either half or across the split. With delta from the half-solutions, inspect points in a width-2delta strip around the dividing line.

syllabus.title: Pivots, selection and search
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Partition separates keys around a pivot, then recurse on the remaining regions. Unlike merge sort, quicksort does its linear organizing work before recursive sorting.

syllabus.title: Sorting choices and lower bounds
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Bubble sort compares adjacent keys and swaps inverted neighbors. A full left-to-right pass moves the largest remaining key to the right boundary.

syllabus.title: Graph exploration
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. An adjacency list uses O(V+E) storage. A V-by-V adjacency matrix uses Theta(V squared) storage and offers constant-time edge lookup.

syllabus.title: DFS structure and dependencies
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. DFS timestamps increase on discovery and finish. Two vertex intervals are either nested, showing ancestry, or disjoint; they never partially overlap.

syllabus.title: Breadth-first paths and coloring
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. BFS marks vertices when enqueuing and processes a FIFO queue. In an unweighted graph, a vertex’s layer number is its shortest-path distance in edges from the source.

syllabus.title: Greedy shortest paths and queues
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. A greedy method makes a locally preferred choice and commits to it. Correctness needs a task-specific argument; choosing the best-looking local option is not automatically globally optimal.

syllabus.title: Shortest paths with signed costs
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. A DAG can have negative edge weights without a cycle. Process vertices in topological order and relax each outgoing edge once to obtain single-source shortest paths in O(V+E) time.

syllabus.title: Minimum-cost spanning networks
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph with no cycle and minimum total edge weight. It has V-1 edges and is a different objective from shortest source-to-vertex paths.

syllabus.title: Prim and tree exchanges
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Distinct edge weights imply a unique MST, but tied weights do not automatically imply multiple MSTs. Exchange an edge along its fundamental cycle to test whether an equally cheap alternative exists.

syllabus.title: Prefix codes and merge costs
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. A binary prefix code assigns symbols to tree leaves. No symbol’s code is a prefix of another, so a bit stream can be decoded by walking from the root to a leaf and restarting.

syllabus.title: Scheduling and divisible items
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Unweighted interval scheduling maximizes the number of nonoverlapping activities on one resource. With half-open intervals, an activity beginning exactly when another ends is compatible.

syllabus.title: Reusable states and stair problems
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Dynamic programming defines states and transitions, then saves overlapping subproblem results. Memoization computes states on demand; tabulation processes them in a dependency-respecting order.

syllabus.title: Longest common subsequences
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. A subsequence retains order but may skip characters. An LCS is a longest sequence shared by two strings; it is not required to be a contiguous substring.

syllabus.title: Matrix-chain optimization
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. Matrix-chain optimization changes parentheses, not matrix order. Multiplying a p-by-q matrix by a q-by-r matrix costs pqr scalar multiplications and yields a p-by-r result.

syllabus.title: Whole-item knapsack
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. In 0-1 knapsack, each item is either taken whole or skipped. The highest value density need not lead to the best whole-item combination; the fractional greedy guarantee does not transfer.

syllabus.title: Reachability, change and route DP
syllabus.goal: Explain the rule, trace a small input, then justify the result. For nonnegative integer values, subset-sum DP records whether each target is reachable by a subset of processed items. The empty subset reaches zero; a descending one-row update prevents item reuse.

syllabus.title: Deadlocks and file systems

courses.name: Database Management Systems
courses.implementation: Prediction introduction, authored guidance, state walkthrough, existing topic lab and misconception notes

syllabus.title: Database foundations and relational thinking
syllabus.goal: Explain what a DBMS does, read relations as structured sets, and protect data with keys and integrity rules.

syllabus.title: Dependencies and normalization
syllabus.goal: Compute attribute closure, identify keys, and decompose relations while checking losslessness and dependency preservation.

syllabus.title: Relational algebra
syllabus.goal: Translate questions into selection, projection, set, join and division operations, then reason about the resulting relation.

syllabus.title: Tuple relational calculus
syllabus.goal: Use tuple variables, predicates and quantifiers to express safe declarative queries and read exam-style expressions.

syllabus.title: SQL querying
syllabus.goal: Write SQL with clear clause order, correct NULL and aggregate behavior, and carefully scoped nested queries.

syllabus.title: Disks and file organization
syllabus.goal: Estimate disk access cost, compare scheduling and file layouts, and track free blocks.

syllabus.title: Indexes and search trees
syllabus.goal: Compare ordered, primary, clustering and secondary indexes, then trace ISAM, B-trees and B+ trees.

syllabus.title: Transactions and serializability
syllabus.goal: Trace reads and writes, apply ACID, and test conflict, view and recoverability properties.

syllabus.title: Concurrency control
syllabus.goal: Apply two-phase locking and timestamp ordering, recognize deadlocks, and compare prevention and recovery choices.

syllabus.title: Entity-relationship design
syllabus.goal: Identify entities, attributes, relationships and weak entities, then map an ER design into relational tables.

syllabus.title: Transport and TCP control

syllabus.title: Traffic and application protocols
